newsitem.title: USA: Solar storm may disrupt satellites, power systems.
newsitem.headline: Solar storm may disrupt satellites, power systems.

text.p: A magnetic cloud blasted from the sun hurtled toward Earth on Wednesday packing radiation that could disrupt communications satellites and power grids, space scientists said.

"It's clearly a big event," said Don Savage, a spokesman for the U.S. National Aeronautics and Space Administration. He compared it with a January 6 solar storm that may have caused the failure of a $200 million AT&T Corp. communications satellite.

Scientists could not immediately say whether the plasma belched by the sun -- as much as 1 million tons of ionised particles moving at up to 3 million miles an hour -- would actually hit the magnetosphere, the Earth's protective magnetic cocoon.

Even if radiation from the so-called coronal mass ejection belted the Earth, it posed no direct physical danger to people, experts said. They said the geomagnetic storm that may result could last from 12 to 48 hours and start late Wednesday.

Barbara Thompson, a solar physicist at the NASA Goddard Space Flight Centre in Greenbelt, Maryland, said the chief threat was to satellites, generators, power grids and other systems that rely on electro-magnetics.

"These events have been impacting the earth for a very long time," she said in a telephone interview, referring to solar storms. "The vulnerability we have ... is that we are becoming increasingly dependent" on satellite communications.
Power companies in the United States and Canada said they were bracing for a solar storm that, if severe, could knock out generating and transmission systems.

"It has the potential to produce a severe impact on the power system ... and the potential to produce large area blackouts," said John Kappenman, supervisor of transmission power engineering at Minnesota Power in Duluth.
Alan Lazarus, a senior research scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology who was monitoring radiowaves from the explosion, said the blast may miss the Earth altogether.

"Earth is kind of tiny," he said in an interview from the Goddard Space Flight Centre. He said scientists were watching data roll in from a satellite called WIND that hovers at the spot where the Earth's gravity and that of the sun are equal.

The solar storm was detected about 48 hours ago by the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory, a WIND companion satellite that NASA and the European Space Agency launched in 1995 to keep a constant eye on the sun's surface.

NASA scientists said the most noticeable impact on the earth may be expanded visibility of the dazzling light shows in the sky called the aurora borealis and aurora australis, which typically can be seen over the north and south poles.

"We might be able to see a neat light show," Thompson said. She estimated the chances were five to one against any geomagnetic storm causing any major disruptions to communications satellites, power grids or other advanced systems.

In the worst recent geomagnetic storm caused by "space weather," Hydro Quebec, a Canadian utility, was plunged into a blackout on March 13, 1989, nearly toppling the power grid in the U.S. Northeast..

In January 1994, a multimillion-volt solar storm knocked out Canada's main television broadcast satellite, Anik E2. The storm damaged the momentum wheel, leaving the "bird" spinning aimlessly in orbit until it was recovered six months later.

The latest big solar storm might have gone largely unnoticed but for the new fleet of international satellites positioned between the earth and sun partly to monitor such events. "The difference is that we actually can see them as they are erupting and evolving," Thompson said.
